clinicalPearls: A proposed inherited thrombophilia characterised by platelet hyperaggregability in response to low concentrations of ADP and adrenaline (epinephrine)
Associated in the literature with arterial and venous thrombosis, often at a young age and sometimes precipitated by emotional or physical stress
Reported clinical events include unexplained stroke, myocardial infarction, and recurrent pregnancy loss in the absence of other thrombophilias
The defining laboratory feature is increased platelet aggregation to low-dose agonists on light transmission aggregometry
It remains a debated and incompletely standardised entity, with no consensus genetic marker and variable diagnostic criteria
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, made after established inherited and acquired thrombophilias have been considered
When treatment is used, it is typically directed at reducing platelet reactivity with antiplatelet therapy rather than anticoagulation alone
reference.pathophysiology: Sticky platelet syndrome is described as a heritable tendency of platelets to aggregate excessively when exposed to low concentrations of ADP and adrenaline, suggesting heightened responsiveness of platelet activation pathways. This hyperreactivity is proposed to promote platelet-driven thrombus formation in both the arterial and venous circulations, particularly under conditions of physiological stress with catecholamine surges. The precise molecular basis is unresolved, no single causative gene has been established, and the entity remains debated, so it is best regarded as a clinico-laboratory phenotype pending further validation.
additionalDifferentials: Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A thrombophilias
Antithrombin, protein C, and protein S deficiencies
Myeloproliferative neoplasms causing thrombocytosis and thrombosis
Acquired prothrombotic states such as malignancy or oestrogen exposure
additionalInvestigations: Light transmission platelet aggregometry using low concentrations of ADP and adrenaline
Comprehensive inherited thrombophilia screen (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C and S)
Full blood count to exclude a myeloproliferative neoplasm
Imaging to confirm and characterise a suspected thrombotic event
redFlags: Arterial thrombosis such as stroke or myocardial infarction in a young patient
Recurrent venous thromboembolism without an obvious cause
Recurrent pregnancy loss after exclusion of other causes
Thrombosis recurring despite an otherwise negative thrombophilia workup
reference.prognosis: Because the entity is not firmly established, prognosis is uncertain; reported cases suggest that reducing platelet reactivity can lessen thrombotic events, but the evidence base is limited. Outcomes are strongly influenced by coexisting, better-defined thrombotic risk factors.
pitfalls: Diagnosing it without first excluding established inherited and acquired thrombophilias
Relying on non-standardised aggregometry protocols with variable cut-offs
Overinterpreting transient platelet hyperreactivity from recent stress or sampling artefact
Attributing all thrombotic events to it while missing a coexisting definitive cause
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
